bibliographic.title: Human–AI hybrid finance: from AI tools to decision systems
bibliographic.authors: Gang Kou; Yan Li; Haomin Wang; Xin Wang
bibliographic.citation_apa: Kou, G., Li, Y., Wang, H., & Wang, X. (2026). Human–AI hybrid finance: from AI tools to decision systems. Financial Innovation, 12, Article 125. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40854-026-00941-w

methodology.study_design: integrative and conceptual review synthesizing literature across finance, management, human-computer interaction (HCI), and AI
methodology.sample_description: literature synthesis across finance, management, HCI, AI, explainability, trust, governance, FinLLMs, agentic finance, and financial regulation
methodology.technology_context: FinLLMs, generative AI, agentic finance, explainable AI, human–AI hybrid financial decision systems

eligibility.decision_rationale: Integrative conceptual review explicitly centered on allocating authority, oversight, and accountability in financial workflows, integrating FinLLMs, generative AI, agentic finance, governance, explainability, and contestability in a regulated finance context. Strong governance and LLM relevance, but conversational/chatbot governance is secondary rather than primary.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Provided text is front matter and selected excerpts only; confirm full-text coverage of conversational interfaces, deployment monitoring, and stated review limitations.

appraisal.notes: Clear integrative review objective and stated inclusion domains (HCI, XAI, governance, FinLLM/GenAI, regulation). Search strategy, corpus size, and full limitations are not visible in the provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: The review presents a coherent governance-oriented framework for human–AI finance with direct FinLLM/GenAI and oversight/contestability content, but appraisal is limited by incomplete full-text access to search methods, corpus boundaries, and explicit limitations.

coding.theme: Governance of human–AI hybrid financial decision systems
coding.subtheme: Oversight, accountability, and explainability for FinLLMs and agentic finance

synthesis.main_claim: AI in finance is shifting from a predictive tool to a component of human–AI hybrid financial decision systems, and the central research question is decision architecture: how authority, oversight, and accountability should be allocated across financial workflows.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes an integrated decision-system framework with five connected constructs—delegation frontier, reliance wedge, decision-useful XAI, meaningful oversight, and reflexive AI loop—to organize research on investment, trading, credit, asset management, risk, compliance, and financial regulation.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence for governance, oversight, accountability, explainability, and contestability in regulated finance involving FinLLMs, generative AI, and agentic systems; not a primary source for conversational-interface-specific governance.

evidence.excerpt: Human–AI hybrid finance: from AI tools to decision systems Gang Kou1, Yan Li2, Haomin Wang3 and Xin Wang1*

evidence.claim: Study is an integrative conceptual review
evidence.excerpt: This integrative and conceptual review synthesizes literature across finance, management, human–computer interaction (HCI), and AI

evidence.claim: Central governance question on authority, oversight, and accountability
evidence.excerpt: the central question is moving from model performance to decision architecture: how authority, oversight, and accountability should be allocated across financial workflows.

evidence.claim: Human–AI complementarity is conditional and governance-dependent
evidence.excerpt: human–AI complementarity in finance is conditional rather than automatic, depending on task structure, private information, feedback quality, incentives, explanation design, and governance.

evidence.claim: Review integrates FinLLMs and agentic finance with governance framework
evidence.excerpt: integrates evidence on methods, data, scenarios, explainability, trust, governance, financial large language models (FinLLMs), and agentic finance

integrated decision-system framework consisting of five connected constructs—delegation frontier, reliance wedge, decision-useful explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), meaningful oversight, and reflexive AI loop
support cumulative research on investment, trading, credit, asset management, risk, compliance, and financial regulation.
AI in finance expanded into supervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and large language models (LLMs), including financial large language models (FinLLMs)

evidence.claim: Finance is highly exposed to generative AI
evidence.excerpt: Finance is also one of the domains most exposed to generative AI (GenAI) because it is information-intensive, text heavy, highly codified, and operationally dependent on rapid judgment under uncertainty

evidence.claim: Review inclusion domains include governance and contestability
evidence.excerpt: Explainable AI, trustworthy AI, and governance research is included to examine transparency, accountability, oversight, and contestability.

evidence.claim: FinLLM/GenAI/agentic AI included as workflow and action layer
evidence.excerpt: FinLLM, generative AI, and agentic AI studies are included because they show how AI is becoming a language, workflow, and action layer in finance.

evidence.claim: Financial regulation included for institutional governance linkage
evidence.excerpt: Financial regulation and systemic-risk work is included where it helps connect AI-mediated decisions to institutional governance

evidence.claim: GenAI extends AI into language, interaction, and workflow
evidence.excerpt: FinLLMs and GenAI extend AI into language, interaction, and workflow.

evidence.claim: LLM reliance should vary by task type
evidence.excerpt: An analyst should not rely on an LLM equally for factual retrieval, causal inference, and valuation judgment.

evidence.claim: High-stakes decisions require understanding, contestation, audit, and accountability
evidence.excerpt: help determine whether AI-mediated decisions can be understood, contested, audited, and assigned to accountable parties.

evidence.claim: LLM-generated outputs pose governance risks in finance
evidence.excerpt: an LLM may generate a misleading investment memo; and an agent may take actions that are difficult to reconstruct.

evidence.claim: Explanation design must be governed, especially for LLMs
evidence.excerpt: explanation design must be governed, not merely deployed. LLMs make this issue sharper because they can generate fluent rationales that sound authoritative without being tied to the actual decision process.
